name: Ben Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy car and van parts for Tri-County Parts Supply, which delivers to around 300 garages. Brake pads, filters, batteries, wiper blades, thousands of lines. I'm on the phone with manufacturers' reps in the morning and in the stock system after lunch, looking at what's moving. I like that I can walk down to the warehouse and see what I've bought. What I don't like is the end-of-month stock count, which makes everyone grumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I'd expected. I'd tell the lads at the five-a-side game that it's another new gadget and we'll all get a bit of use from it. I'd keep it short and a bit dry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. Dee, my wife, is a dental hygienist and her work's steady, the house is paid off nearly, and we've a good cushion. My own job's the kind where you can't skip a day, since garages need parts every morning, and I'd be glad if that stayed true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd use the chat tool a bit more for the dull things, like the draft supplier emails and the monthly report. I'd sit down with the stock system's new reorder suggestions and compare them against my own gut for a few months, to see which wins. Retirement is planned for 62 or 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. Settled. I'd feel the same as I do on a day when the stock count comes out right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the stock count. What is it about the count that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been using the chat tool for about a year, for emails and for summarising the long supplier catalogues. It saves me maybe an hour a day, though it gets part numbers wrong, so I always check. That's the bit that keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the reorder suggestions against your gut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the suggestions match my gut, I'd trust them more. I'll trust the software's reorder suggestions once they beat my gut for six months in a row, and not before. If they don't, I'll ask why, and I'll probably find out the software missed something.

say: I'd say it's **another gadget** and we'll all get some use from it.
I'd keep it short and dry with the lads at five-a-side.
think: Dee's work is steady, our house is nearly paid and we have a good **cushion**.
Garages need parts **every morning**, and I hope that stays true.
do: Use the chat tool more for **emails** and the monthly report.
Compare the reorder **suggestions** with my own gut for a few months.
feel: **Settled**, like a day when the stock count comes out right.
S0.quote: I'll trust the software's reorder suggestions once they beat my gut for six months in a row, and not before.
fieldNote: Ben is already an occasional AI user, treating it as a modest, checkable helper.
He wants to test the software against his own **judgement**, which fits a steady adopter.
Calm because the household income is stable and savings are strong.

steps.text: Use the chat tool for supplier emails and the monthly report
Test the stock system's reorder suggestions against my own gut for six months
Keep buying as usual and plan to retire at 62 or 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, well, it's coming, so let's pick the parts of it that work. I'd tell the younger buyers that they can't just trust the output. To my five-a-side mates I'd say my job's going to look different in three years, and so is theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think around a third of what I do moves to software: checking stock, setting reorder points, comparing prices across suppliers. What stays is the parts nobody puts in a database, like which brand's brake pads get returned, and which rep's promises are real. I think there'll be fewer of us, maybe two buyers instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the trial of the new system and sit with the supplier's consultants to make sure it fits our business. I'd start learning how to check the machine's orders properly and how to spot a daft one. And I'd keep a quarter of my bonus aside, because if the team shrinks, the bonus is the first thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, honestly. It's not fear, it's the feeling of a good routine being loosened. I'm 58, so I think about whether to go along with it or step aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior buyer, Dana. She's 29 and sharp, but the work she does, the price comparisons, is exactly what goes first. I'd teach her the supplier relationship side, the phone and the trust, and I'd tell her to ask for the lead on the next trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd consider stepping aside. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be talking to management about who stays and who goes. Software will do the stock checking and the price comparing, but it'll never know which rep's promise is real and which one's a bluff. It's not good for me to say, but I'd say it anyway.

I'd tell younger buyers they can't just **trust** the output.
think: About a **third** of my work moves to software: stock, reorder points and price checks.
I expect two buyers instead of **three**.
do: Ask to lead the **trial** of the new system.
Learn to **check** the machine's orders and spot a daft one.
Keep a quarter of my **bonus** aside in case the team shrinks.
feel: A bit **unsettled**, like a good routine being loosened.
S1.quote: Software will do the stock checking and the price comparing, but it'll never know which rep's promise is real and which one's a bluff.
fieldNote: Ben expects the team to shrink but also expects to stay on the **right side** of it as the person who checks.
His concern for the junior buyer Dana is practical: teach her the relationship half.
Uneasy rather than anxious because he is adaptive enough and well-cushioned.

steps.text: Ask to lead the trial of the new buying system
Learn to spot a daft order from the machine and check it
Set aside a quarter of my bonus in case the team shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got two years to get this right, and that's not nearly enough. At work I'd say no one should be let go in a panic. To friends, I'd say it's the first time the whole country's in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone within two years, and a few months after the thinking part. The garages might keep a person to deal with a human face, but not from a wholesaler's head office. I'd say I have maybe a year and a half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as long as I'm useful, then ask for a package. I'd take the pension lump sum at the earliest allowed date, and I'd put a chunk into index funds. I'd also train as a motor-vehicle inspector on a short course, a hands-on job in the same trade. Dee would carry on working, and we'd cut back on the big holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, no point denying it. But I'm the sort who goes and does something, so I'd feel better once I'd booked the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Josh is a mechanic, which is hands-on, so he has the extra time. I'd tell him not to take on any big debts. I'd also tell him that he could take over my little fund for a workshop if he wanted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd train as an inspector. Why that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the kind of person who feels better once I've booked a course, so I'd sign up for the inspector training the same week. I'd rather have a part-time hands-on job than a big pay cheque I can't count on.

say: I'd say two years isn't nearly enough and nobody should be let go in a **panic**.
I'd tell friends the whole country is in the **same boat**.
think: My buying job is **gone** within two years, perhaps a few months after the thinking part.
I might keep a year and a half, **at best**.
do: Ask for a **package** when the time comes.
Put a chunk of savings into **index funds**.
Train as a motor-vehicle **inspector** on a short course.
feel: **Anxious**, but better once I've booked the course.
S2.quote: I'm the kind of person who feels better once I've booked a course, so I'd sign up for the inspector training the same week.
fieldNote: Ben expects the buying job to go in about two years but acts quickly to find a hands-on role.
His **inspector** plan is realistic: same trade, physical work, with robots three years later.
He thinks of his mechanic son Josh and offers help rather than advice only.

steps.text: Ask for a redundancy package when the buying team is cut
Sign up for a short motor-vehicle inspector course
Put a chunk of savings into index funds
Cut back on the big holiday and keep a year's cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something you can plan with. At work I'd get people to list what would go and what stays. To friends I'd say, it's like a long road closure: you can see it, so you plan the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably be gone by then. I'd be 63, and I'd leave with my pension. But I'd think about Dana and the younger ones, and whether I'd done enough for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, and I'd use the five years to learn the tools properly. I'd start a little part-time consulting for garage owners who want help choosing a supplier. I'd also take the plan to Dee: we'd pay down the mortgage and put aside money for Josh, in case his workshop idea goes ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad. A bit uneasy, but that's normal. The sky isn't falling in the five-year version, it's more like grey weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company to do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for training on the new system now, not later, and for it to cover everyone. I'd say to management: look, if they're going to cut the buying team, say so in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the consulting for garage owners involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is like a long road closure: you can see it coming, so you plan the route instead of sitting in the queue. I'd want the date to be written in a document, not whispered in a corridor.

say: I'd say five years is something you can **plan** with.
I'd get colleagues to list what goes and what **stays**.
think: I'd probably be **gone** by then, at 63 with my pension.
I'd worry whether I'd done enough for **Dana** and the younger buyers.
do: Use the five years to learn the tools **properly**.
Start part-time **consulting** for garage owners choosing suppliers.
Pay down the **mortgage** and set aside money for Josh.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, like grey weather rather than a falling sky.
S3.quote: Five years is like a long road closure: you can see it coming, so you plan the route instead of sitting in the queue.
fieldNote: Five years lets Ben plan calmly; his main concern is the younger buyers.
He wants clear **dates in writing** from management.
The consulting idea is a modest, plausible side income.

steps.text: Learn the buying tools properly over the next two years
Start part-time consulting for garage owners choosing suppliers
Pay down the mortgage and set aside money for Josh's workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and plenty of time to get ready. I'd say to friends that we'll all have a bit of a shake-up but we have time. At work I'd just say let's keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it won't touch my job, as I'd have retired. It touches Josh and Dana and the whole country. I'd be a bit relaxed about it all, but I wouldn't be cocky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, using the tools more each year. I'd retire at 63 and then do some part-time work in the garages, helping out with the paperwork. I'd put a little money into Josh's workshop, and keep the rest in the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the kind of thing you read about and then get on with your day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dana, your younger colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get a trade that you can do with your hands, because it's the safe side for the time being. But I'd also say be careful, because three years isn't a lot either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years isn't a lot. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty of time to get ready, as long as people actually start in the first one. It's still a good rule of thumb.

say: I'd say ten years is a long **runway** with plenty of time to get ready.
I'd tell friends we'll have a **shake-up** but we have time.
think: It won't touch my job, as I'd have **retired**.
It touches Josh, Dana and the **whole country**, and I wouldn't know what to tell them.
do: Retire at **63**, then do part-time paperwork for garages.
Put a little money into **Josh's** workshop.
feel: **Calm**, the sort of thing you read about and then get on with your day.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty of time to get ready, as long as people actually start in the first one.
fieldNote: At ten years Ben is calm; his own job ends before the change.
He suggests **hands-on** trades as the safe side, while noting robots follow about three years later.
Plans modest support for Josh's workshop.

steps.text: Use the buying tools more each year until I retire at 63
Do part-time paperwork for local garages after I retire
Put a little money into Josh's workshop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too fast for anyone, including me. What would help is clear dates from the company, paid retraining and decent pension protection, so people aren't forced to go early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. I'd say that I'm usually the optimist, but I'd want the answers in writing. I'd rather have a part-time hands-on job I can count on than a big pay cheque I can't.

headlineQuote: I'd rather have a part-time hands-on job I can count on than a big pay cheque I can't.
portrait: Ben is **58**, a parts buyer at Tri-County Parts Supply, who uses the chat tool now and then and checks everything.
He's centrist and practical, preferring to **test** a new tool against his own judgement.
He stays calm when the change is slow, and responds to the fast worlds by booking **courses** and planning.
He thinks of his young colleague Dana and his mechanic son Josh in every scenario.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, which is too fast for anyone to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **dates** from the company, paid retraining and pension protection.
